title: pandas Foundations: Completed Activity
text:
Reflection
The written request supplies three row conditions, five output columns, and two sorting priorities. The code preserves that structure: the mask defines which talks qualify, .loc[] retains the requested fields, and sort_values() puts year ahead of word count when ordering the result.

title: pandas
text:
A request about 794 talks
You receive a table with 794 General Conference talks and 14 variables.

Find the five talks from 2018 through 2020 with the largest word counts. Show the title, speaker, conference, and word count.


What must your code do before you can answer?


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Read the request without showing code. Ask students to name the decisions hidden inside it. Listen for understanding rows and columns, filtering years, choosing columns, sorting, and keeping five rows.

title: pandas
text:
Think, pair, share


What does one row need to represent?
Which variables matter for the request?
Which observations qualify?
How should the qualifying rows be ordered?
What would you check before reporting the answer?



Planned time: 4 minutes.
Give students about 45 seconds to think and 90 seconds to compare. During the share, collect one answer for each question. Keep the discussion at the level of table operations rather than pandas syntax.

title: pandas
section: A data question becomes table operations
text:
A data question becomes table operations

Understand: identify the observational unit and variables.
Select: keep the columns needed for the answer.
Filter: keep the rows that satisfy the conditions.
Order: arrange the rows so the requested cases come first.
Check: confirm the shape and meaning of the result.


pandas gives these operations a vocabulary.


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Use this as the debrief for the discussion. The five verbs organize the rest of the lecture. Point out that the order of selecting and filtering can vary, but every operation should serve the question.

title: pandas
text:
Today’s problem

How can we translate a question about tabular data into explicit operations on labeled rows and columns?

By the end of class, you should be able to reason about:

Series and DataFrames
labels, positions, and alignment
selecting and filtering observations
sorting by one or more variables
vectorized variables and simple summaries


Planned time: 1 minute.
This is the roadmap. Tell students that the opening request will return in the repository activity.

title: pandas
text:
What pandas adds

Row and column labels carry meaning into the code.
Each column can have its own data type.
Labels support selection and automatic alignment.
Table methods express common data tasks directly.


Shape, vectorization, and Boolean masks still matter.


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Keep the NumPy connection strong without claiming that every modern pandas column must use an ordinary NumPy array internally. pandas can use additional storage types.
Source: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html

title: pandas
text:
Two core objects


Series
One labeled sequence of values
score_df["exam_1"]
One dimension

DataFrame
Labeled rows and columns
score_df[["exam_1", "exam_3"]]
Two dimensions


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Describe a DataFrame as a collection of aligned Series. The single bracket and double bracket distinction will return later with visible results.

title: pandas
text:
Labels participate in computation
first_exam = pd.Series(
    [82, 75], index=["Ana", "Bo"]
)

bonus = pd.Series(
    [5, 2], index=["Bo", "Ana"]
)

What should first_exam + bonus return?


Planned time: 1 minute.
Ask students to predict before revealing the result. NumPy-style positional addition would suggest 87 and 77. pandas uses the labels.

title: pandas
text:
pandas aligns matching labels
first_exam + bonus

Ana    84
Bo     80
dtype: int64


Ana receives Ana’s bonus even though the Series use different orders.


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Read the calculation for each student. Label alignment prevents values from silently changing meaning when their order differs. Mention that missing labels introduce missing results, but leave missingness for its dedicated lesson.
Source: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html

title: pandas
text:
Apply the mask with .loc[]
recent_talks = talks.loc[
    recent_mask,
    ["talk_name", "speaker", "conference", "year", "num_words"]
]

The expression before the comma selects rows.
The list after the comma selects columns.
The result has 201 rows and 5 columns.


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Read the expression aloud as keep rows where the recent mask is true, then keep these five labeled columns. This makes the two-axis structure explicit.

title: pandas
text:
Combining conditions
mask = (
    talks["year"].between(2019, 2020)
    & (talks["session"] == "sunday-morning")
    & talks["num_words"].between(1400, 1700)
)

& means elementwise AND.
| means elementwise OR.
~ reverses a Boolean condition.
Parentheses make each comparison explicit.


Planned time: 3 minutes.
Explain why ordinary Python and, or, and not do not make one decision per row. Do not dwell on operator precedence rules. Teach parentheses as the readable standard.

title: pandas
text:
Helpers express common conditions


Inclusive range
talks["year"].between(2018, 2020)

Set membership
talks["session"].isin([
    "sunday-morning",
    "sunday-afternoon"
])


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Show the longer equivalent only verbally if useful. These helpers often express the data question more clearly than a long chain of repeated comparisons.

title: pandas
text:
Three filtering mistakes
# Python asks for one truth value
condition_1 and condition_2

# The comparisons need parentheses
talks["year"] >= 2018 & talks["year"] <= 2020

# This assignment targets a temporary result
talks[talks["year"] >= 2018]["recent"] = True

Use vectorized operators, parenthesized comparisons, and one .loc[] assignment.


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Do not ask students to memorize warning messages. Emphasize the reliable pattern. With pandas 3 Copy-on-Write, chained assignment never updates the original object.
Sources:

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/indexing.html
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/copy_on_write.html

Which rows qualify?

Sorting asks:

In what order should the qualifying rows appear?

recent_talks.sort_values("num_words")

Ascending order is the default.


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Connect sorting to the opening request. The qualifying rows do not change. Only their displayed order changes.

longest_recent = (
    recent_talks
    .sort_values("num_words", ascending=False)
    .head(5)
)

ascending=False places larger values first.
head(5) keeps the first five rows after sorting.

Planned time: 2 minutes.
Ask what would happen if head(5) came before sorting. It would return the largest values only by accident. The sequence of operations carries meaning.

    "num_words", ascending=False

Recommend named steps while students are learning and debugging. Each name gives them a checkpoint where they can inspect shape and content.

section: The same logic as a chain
text:
The same logic as a chain
answer = (
    talks.loc[
        talks["year"].between(2018, 2020),
        ["talk_name", "speaker", "conference", "num_words"]
    ]
    .sort_values("num_words", ascending=False)
    .head(5)
)

Read the chain from top to bottom as a sequence of table operations.


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Students should be able to read this chain today. They do not need to prefer it over named intermediate objects yet.

title: pandas
text:
Translate the request into pandas

Find Sunday morning talks from 2019 or 2020 with 1,400 through 1,700 words. Keep the title, speaker, conference, year, and word count. Put newer years first, then longer talks within each year.

With a partner, identify:

the row conditions
the selected columns
the ordering columns and directions
one result check


Planned time: 4 minutes.
Give pairs two minutes. Ask them to explain the operation sequence before writing exact syntax. A useful check is that every returned row should have a Sunday morning session, an allowed year, and a word count inside the inclusive range.

title: pandas
text:
A defensible translation
mask = (
    talks["year"].between(2019, 2020)
    & (talks["session"] == "sunday-morning")
    & talks["num_words"].between(1400, 1700)
)

selected = talks.loc[
    mask,
    ["talk_name", "speaker", "conference", "year", "num_words"]
]

result = selected.sort_values(
    ["year", "num_words"],
    ascending=[False, False]
)

Planned time: 2 minutes.
Use this as the immediate summary. Point to the one-to-one relationship between the prose request and each part of the code.

Planned time: 10 to 15 minutes.
Pause after checkpoints 2, 3, and 5. Ask students to compare types, shapes, and row counts. If class time is short, complete the first three checkpoints together and release students for the final request.

title: pandas
text:
What pandas contributed

Labels kept variables connected to their meanings.
A Boolean Series made one filtering decision per talk.
.loc[] selected rows and columns together.
sort_values() expressed priority and tie-breaking.
Vectorized expressions created values for every row.


Planned time: 2 minutes.
Ask students to name the operation that served each part of the activity request before revealing the bullets.

title: pandas
text:
Exit check
For each line, predict the result type or meaning:
talks["speaker"]

talks[["speaker"]]

talks.loc[talks["year"] == 2020, ["speaker", "talk_name"]]

talks.sort_values(
    ["year", "num_words"],
    ascending=[True, False]
)

Planned time: 3 minutes.
Expected responses: Series, one-column DataFrame, a two-column DataFrame containing 2020 talks, and a DataFrame ordered from earlier to later years with larger word counts first within each year.

title: pandas
text:
pandas’ organizing idea

A DataFrame keeps values connected to labels, and a clear analysis translates a question into inspectable table operations.


Know what one row represents.
Predict the type and shape of each intermediate result.
Check that the final rows and columns answer the original question.


Planned time: 1 minute.
End with the reasoning habit rather than a list of methods. The next lesson can build on this foundation by asking how to summarize separate groups of rows.
